structure.summary:

- Table of contents: Comprehensive listing of Parts I–IV, including Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for Common Equity and Issuer Purchases; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Controls and Procedures; and other required items and exhibits.
- Business overview (Part I, Item 1):
  - Company profile: Global security and aerospace company focused on research, design, development, manufacture, integration, and sustainment of advanced technology systems, plus engineering, logistics, systems integration, and cybersecurity services. Principal customers are U.S. Government agencies; products and services also have international, civil, and commercial applications.
  - Strategic vision: “21st Century Security” — integrating new and existing systems across all domains using advanced, open-architecture networking and operational technologies to increase agility and effectiveness.
  - Near- to mid-term growth pillars: 
    - Current programs of record (e.g., F-35 sustainment; increased PAC-3 production; CH-53K; Trident II D5 modernization).
    - Classified programs transitioning from development to production over the next few years.
    - Hypersonics programs expected to enter early production between 2023 and 2026.
    - Pursuit of new program awards to expand capabilities and global reach.
  - Enablers: Investment in differentiating technologies; strategic partnerships (including with commercial companies); digital business transformation to enhance infrastructure, efficiency, and collaboration; fiscal discipline; talent development; ongoing internal innovation; and active portfolio management (including potential acquisitions, divestitures, joint ventures, and equity investments).
  - Business segments: Aeronautics; Missiles and Fire Control (MFC); Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS); and Space.
  - Aeronautics segment details: Engages in R&D, production, integration, sustainment, support, and upgrades of advanced military aircraft and UAVs, including classified programs. Major programs include:
    - F-35 Lightning II (multi-role, multi-variant 5th-generation stealth fighter) — the company’s largest program, representing 27% of total consolidated net sales and 66% of Aeronautics’ 2022 net sales; encompasses development (modernization/evolving threats), production, and sustainment (logistics and training).
    - C-130 Hercules (international tactical airlifter).
    - F-16 Fighting Falcon (multi-role fighter).
    - F-22 Raptor (air dominance and multi-role 5th-generation stealth fighter).

structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase:
We are a global security and aerospace company principally engaged in the research, design, development, manufacture, 
integration and sustainment of advanced technology systems, products and services.
structure.summary:
- Overview: A global security and aerospace company focused on research, design, development, manufacture, integration, and sustainment of advanced systems and services. Offers management, engineering, technical, scientific, logistics, system integration, and cybersecurity services. Primary markets include defense, space, intelligence, homeland security, and IT/cybersecurity, serving U.S. and international customers, principally U.S. Government agencies.

- Strategic vision (21st Century Security): Accelerate adoption of advanced networking and leading-edge technologies; integrate new and existing systems across all domains via open-architecture networks and operational technologies to enhance agility, adaptability, and deterrence value.

- Near- to mid-term growth pillars:
  - Current programs of record: growth in F-35 sustainment (Aeronautics), increased PAC-3 production (MFC), CH-53K heavy-lift helicopter (RMS), and Trident II D5 modernization (Space).
  - Classified programs: several in development expected to transition to production over the next few years.
  - Hypersonics: multiple programs moving toward early production between 2023 and 2026 pending successful tests.
  - New awards: ongoing pursuit to expand future platforms and global reach.

- Enablers of strategy: investment in differentiating technologies; strategic partnerships (including with commercial firms); multi-year digital business transformation to improve infrastructure, efficiency, and collaboration; fiscal discipline; substantial workforce and talent development; internal R&D for evolving missions; active portfolio management including selective acquisitions, divestitures, partnerships, joint ventures, and equity investments.

- Business structure: Four segments—Aeronautics; Missiles and Fire Control (MFC); Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS); Space.

- Aeronautics segment: Develops and supports advanced military aircraft (combat, air mobility), unmanned air vehicles, and related technologies, including classified programs. Major programs:
  - F-35 Lightning II (multi-role, multi-variant fifth-generation stealth fighter)
  - C-130 Hercules (tactical airlifter)
  - F-16 Fighting Falcon (multi-role fighter)
  - F-22 Raptor (air dominance/multi-role fifth-generation fighter)

- F-35 program highlights: Company’s largest program—27% of total consolidated net sales and 66% of Aeronautics’ net sales in 2022. Encompasses development (modernization and countering emerging threats), production, and sustainment (logistics and training) for global customers.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: ITEM 1. Business
structure.start_phrase:
We are a global security and aerospace company principally engaged in the research, design, development, manufacture, 
integration and sustainment of advanced technology systems, products and services.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: A global security and aerospace contractor focused on defense, space, intelligence, homeland security, and IT (including cybersecurity), primarily serving U.S. Government agencies with additional international civil and commercial applications.
- Strategy and vision: “21st Century Security” aims to integrate platforms across domains via open-architecture networking, advanced technologies, and partnerships. Near- to mid‑term growth drivers include current programs of record, classified programs, hypersonics, and new awards. Emphasis on digital transformation, commercial partnerships, disciplined capital allocation, portfolio shaping, and talent development.
- Operating structure: Four segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space.
  - Aeronautics: Designs, produces, sustains advanced military aircraft; major programs F-35 (27% of total net sales, 66% of Aeronautics in 2022), C-130, F-16, F-22; Advanced Development Programs (Skunk Works) on next-gen air dominance, hypersonics, ISR, autonomy, and networking.
  - MFC: Air/missile defense (PAC-3, THAAD), tactical/strike missiles (MLRS/HIMARS, JASSM, Hellfire), fire control (Apache, SNIPER, IRST21), logistics (SOF GLSS), hypersonics, and Javelin JV with Raytheon.
  - RMS: Military/commercial helicopters (BLACK HAWK, Seahawk, CH‑53K, CRH, VH‑92A), integrated warfare systems and sensors (Aegis, LCS/MMSC), C6ISR (C2BMC, undersea combat systems), training and logistics solutions.
  - Space: Satellites and space systems (SBIRS/Next Gen OPIR, GPS III, Orion), strategic systems (Trident II D5 FBM, NGI), hypersonics, classified national security programs; AWE UK program renationalized in 2021 and removed from results.
- Intellectual property: Extensive patents, trademarks, trade secrets; U.S. and non‑U.S. governments retain certain IP rights under FAR/DFARS and similar regimes; no single IP right is material to the company as a whole.
- Research and development: Both company‑funded (IR&D) and customer‑funded R&D to advance technologies and upgrade products; costs include research through test activities.
- Supply chain and materials: Uses scarce materials (aluminum, titanium, carbon fiber) with long‑term agreements; relies on suppliers for components (semiconductors, microelectronics). COVID‑19 and global chip shortages in 2022 caused delays, higher costs, and performance impacts; effects expected to continue into 2023. No material seasonality, but timing of awards, funding, deliveries, and acceptances can shift sales between periods.
- Human capital: Approximately 116,000 employees (as of Dec 31, 2022), ~93% U.S.-based; ~60,000 engineers/scientists/IT; ~19% under collective bargaining; positive labor relations. Diversity and inclusion initiatives with Business Resource Groups; U.S. workforce profile—Women 23%, People of Color 30%, Veterans 21%, People with Disabilities 11%; executives—Women 25%, People of Color 16%, Veterans 21%, People with Disabilities 11% (self-identified). Focus on early‑career hiring, retention, engagement, flexible telework, training, and leadership development. Safety/health programs maintained; COVID‑19 protocols and impacts noted.
- Competition: Faces intense domestic and international competition (Boeing, General Dynamics, L3Harris, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, smaller firms, startups, and non‑traditional entrants). Frequent teaming with competitors; factors include technical performance, cost, innovation, execution, reputation, and global access. International sales influenced by U.S. export rules, local laws, offsets, and industrial cooperation.
- Government contracts and regulations: Highly regulated environment under U.S. and foreign rules (FAR/DFARS). Requirements include cost/pricing disclosures, specialized accounting, allowable cost rules, cybersecurity controls, export controls/classification, prohibited source restrictions, and government reviews of business systems. Contracts can be terminated for convenience or default. Use of undefinitized contract actions (UCAs) can affect pricing/profit and cash flow. Classified work has similar risks to other U.S. Government contracts, with unique insurance limitations. Environmental compliance obligations exist; costs largely recoverable under U.S. contracts.
- Climate and sustainability: Monitoring evolving GHG/climate regulations (e.g., carbon taxes, mandatory disclosures, procurement preferences); sustainability program includes targets to reduce GHG emissions; potential for higher compliance costs.
- Corporate and investor information: Formed in 1995 (Lockheed + Martin Marietta); HQ in Bethesda, MD; SEC filings available on company and SEC websites; website content not incorporated by reference.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary statements and safe harbor disclosures regarding projections, assumptions, and risks.
- Key risk factor highlighted: Heavy reliance on U.S. Government spending (73% of 2022 net sales; 64% from DoD). Budget uncertainty, continuing resolutions, shutdowns, debt ceiling issues, and shifting priorities may delay/cut funding, restrict new starts, or cancel programs; development-to-production transitions (e.g., hypersonics, classified programs) depend on authorization/funding. Many contracts are incrementally funded; costs incurred beyond obligated amounts risk non‑reimbursement.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: ITEM 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements caution and safe harbor: projections are uncertain, subject to risks, and not to be relied upon for investment decisions; no obligation to update except as required by law.
- Item 1A Risk Factors overview: extensive risks that could materially affect operating results, financial position, and cash flows.
- Reliance on U.S. Government contracts: 73% of 2022 sales from U.S. Government (64% DoD); exposure to budget uncertainty, shutdowns, continuing resolutions, and debt ceiling; funding delays, program cancellations, and shifting priorities.
- F-35 program concentration: 27% of 2022 sales; risks from funding cuts/delays, supplier performance, software and testing, modernization, sustainment affordability, inflation, non-compliant parts, GFE engine delivery suspensions, and delivery pauses.
- Procurement laws/regulations: strict compliance requirements, potential penalties, suspension/debarment, export restrictions; government rights to terminate for convenience or default; unique risks of undefinitized contract actions and unilateral definitization; constraints from classified contracts.
- Evolving procurement policies: greater use of fixed-price (including development) and incentive structures, EPA clauses, award fee criteria changes, progress payment changes, and DoD rapid acquisition/OTAs that may limit traditional contractor participation.
- Profitability and cash flow variability: mix of cost-reimbursable vs fixed-price/FPI contracts; risks of cost overruns, schedule/technical issues, reach-forward losses; LRIP transition and option-year uncertainties.
- Government audits and investigations: DCAA/DCMA/IG reviews of pricing, performance, costs, and systems; potential repayments, delays, penalties, and reputational harm.
- Competitive environment and bid protests: increased competition from non-traditional entrants, pricing pressure via IDIQ/multi-award vehicles, internalization by customers, aggressive bidding risks, and protest-related delays (e.g., FLRAA protest).
- Supply chain dependence: performance, quality, compliance, and financial health of subcontractors/teammates; non-compliant parts risk; rare earth sourcing limits; semiconductor shortages; single/sole source constraints; cybersecurity compliance burdens across tiers.
- Technology development and execution: need to innovate rapidly (e.g., JADO, digital/network technologies), supplier dependencies for upgrades, risk of delays/costs in R&D, and digital transformation execution risk; competition from faster/cheaper alternatives; uncertainty in hypersonics/classified/next-gen franchises.
- Macroeconomic risks: inflation, recession, tighter credit, higher interest rates, FX; pressure on fixed-price programs; supplier weakness; pension asset/liability impacts.
- Public health risks: COVID-19 impacts on supply chain, labor, schedules, travel/access restrictions; uncertain future effects on execution and budgets.
- International sales risks (26% of 2022 sales): budget/FX pressures, trade sanctions, intense global competition with foreign government support; compliance with export controls, FCPA/anti-corruption, anti-boycott; higher-risk DCS vs FMS; complex offset/industrial participation obligations and JV dependencies.
- Geopolitical risks: Russia-Ukraine conflict (demand vs supply/funding constraints; cyber threats; supply chain disruptions); potential/actual sanctions (China, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia) impacting sales, supply chain, and programs (e.g., TUHP).
- Intellectual property: government use rights under FAR/DFARS; evolving DoD IP policies; need for supplier licenses; potential third-party infringement claims.
- Workforce and labor: competition for cleared and specialized talent; hybrid work impacts; knowledge transfer/succession; unionized workforce (approx. 19%) and potential work stoppages; supplier labor actions.
- Cybersecurity and physical security: persistent, sophisticated threats (including nation-state actors), insider risks, supply chain cyber vulnerabilities, potential data/IP compromise, operational disruption, compliance and disclosure obligations; limited insurance/indemnities for cyber-related liabilities.
- M&A, JVs, and investments: due diligence, integration, regulatory scrutiny (e.g., Aerojet Rocketdyne termination), successor liability, non-controlling risks, valuation volatility and impairments for strategic investments/funds.
- Pension and postretirement plans: sensitivity to returns, discount rates, mortality; FAS/CAS differences and cash flow timing; contributions and risk-transfer GACs with insurer counterparty risk.
- Estimates and impairments: complex judgments in percentage-of-completion accounting and purchase price allocations; significant goodwill ($10.8B total; Sikorsky ~$3.5B) with impairment risk tied to program outcomes and market conditions.
- Tax risks: law changes and audits; R&D capitalization/amortization beginning 2022 impacting cash taxes; deferred tax asset volatility.
- Insurance/indemnity limits: potential uninsured or underinsured losses, exclusions (e.g., war), natural disasters/climate risks at key sites, and constraints on insuring classified program property.
- Environmental and climate-related risks: remediation liabilities, evolving standards, cost allowability disputes, potential criminal exposure, and emerging climate regulations affecting operations, procurement competitiveness, and litigation risk.
- Legal proceedings: uncertainty of outcomes; reserves based on probability/estimability may change with developments.
- Capital return policies: dividends and share repurchases at Board discretion; subject to legal/financial constraints and may vary from expectations.
- Item 1B: no unresolved SEC staff comments.
- Item 2 Properties: overview of facilities (339 locations, 10 government-owned managed/occupied) and major operating sites by segment in the U.S. and Poland; corporate in Bethesda, Maryland.

structure.start_phrase: The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (MD&A) is intended to help the reader understand our results of operations and financial condition.

- Scope and purpose: MD&A for fiscal 2022 with comparisons to 2021; to be read with consolidated financial statements.
- Company overview: Global security and aerospace contractor focused on defense, space, intelligence, homeland security and IT/cyber; primary customer the U.S. Government. 2022 net sales mix: 73% U.S. Government (64% DoD), 26% international, 1% U.S. commercial. Four segments: Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space.
- Strategy and growth vectors: 21st Century Security vision to network platforms with open architectures; near/mid‑term growth from programs of record (e.g., F‑35 sustainment, PAC‑3, CH‑53K, Trident II D5), classified programs transitioning to production, hypersonics moving toward early production 2023–2026, and pursuit of new awards. Emphasis on tech investment, partnerships (including commercial), digital transformation, portfolio shaping, and disciplined capital allocation.
- Operating environment:
  - COVID‑19: Ongoing supply chain and labor disruptions into 2022; mitigation via $1.5B accelerated supplier payments and on‑site support; some impacts expected to continue into 2023.
  - Inflation/interest rates: Pressure on labor and supplier costs; risk to margins on fixed‑price contracts; pursuing EPA clauses and efficiencies; rising rates increase borrowing costs but reduce gross pension obligations.
  - Russia‑Ukraine conflict: Heightened demand (especially Europe) and U.S. stockpile replenishment; long-cycle nature tempers near-term sales impact; monitoring sanctions, supply chain, and elevated cyber threats.
- Portfolio and notable events:
  - Ongoing M&A/partnership evaluations.
  - UK renationalization of Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) effective June 30, 2021; 2021 had partial-year AWE results only.
- U.S. Government funding: FY23 Omnibus enacted $858B national defense ($816.7B DoD), plus $47B Ukraine supplemental (total $113B since March 2022). FY24 budget and debt ceiling debates introduce uncertainty; defense broadly expected to retain priority but program-level impacts unpredictable.
- International business: Strategy to grow international via FMS (74% of international sales) and DCS (26%). 2022 international sales concentration in Aeronautics, MFC, RMS. Ongoing demand for F‑35, F‑16, C‑130J; PAC‑3/THAAD; Aegis, surface combatants, training/logistics, and Sikorsky platforms.
- F‑35 program status: Strong international momentum (Finland, Switzerland, Germany; Canada selection); finalized LRIP Lots 15–17 for up to 398 aircraft; 2022 deliveries 141; cumulative deliveries 894. Late‑2022 GFE engine issue paused flight ops and deliveries; 2023 production targeted at 147–153 with 156/year targeted from 2025.
- Backlog: $150.0B at 12/31/22 (funded $95.5B), up from $135.4B; ~37% to be recognized within 12 months, ~61% within 24 months.
- Consolidated results (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Net sales: $66.0B, down 1.6% (products $55.5B, services $10.5B); supply chain headwinds weighed on volume.
  - Operating profit: $8.35B, down from $9.12B; gross profit down; RMS severance/impairment charges ($100M).
  - Interest expense up to $623M on new debt for share repurchases.
  - Non‑service FAS pension expense $971M, including $1.5B noncash settlement charge from pension risk transfer; 2021 included $1.7B settlement charge.
  - Other non‑operating swung to ($74M) from $288M on mark‑to‑market investment declines.
  - Effective tax rate 14.2% (R&D credits benefit). New tax rule to amortize R&D raised 2022 cash taxes by ~$660M; expected ~$575M in 2023. Inflation Reduction Act minimum tax/buyback excise expected immaterial.
  - Net earnings: $5.73B ($21.66/share) vs. $6.32B ($22.76); share count lower on buybacks.
- Segment performance (2022):
  - Aeronautics: Sales $27.0B (+1%); OP $2.87B (+2%); higher classified volume and F‑22 profit adjustments; F‑35 volume and net favorable adjustments lower; backlog up on Lot 15/16 awards.
  - MFC: Sales $11.3B (–3%); OP $1.64B (–1%); lower SOF GLSS and SNIPER volume; mixed IAMD (lower THAAD, lower PAC‑3 net favorable adjustments); tactical/strike mixed; backlog up on GMLRS and THAAD.
  - RMS: Sales $16.1B (–4%); OP $1.67B (–7%); lower TLS (non‑recurring 2021 pilot trainer), lower C6ISR and Black Hawk volume; higher CH‑53K; lower net favorable adjustments; backlog up on Sikorsky orders; FLRAA award protested.
  - Space: Sales $11.5B (–2%); OP $1.05B (–8%); AWE roll‑off; lower Orion; higher NGI and classified development; higher ULA equity earnings; lower net favorable adjustments; backlog up on Orion options and national security awards.
  - FAS/CAS pension operating adjustment $1.71B (favorable). Net profit booking rate adjustments added ~$1.8B to segment OP (down from ~$2.0B in 2021); includes ~$780M of unfavorable items.
  - Program risks: Canadian Maritime Helicopter (CH‑148) recovery depends on flight hours; potential contract restructuring. Turkish Utility Helicopter Program affected by U.S. sanctions; possible restructuring/termination.
- Liquidity and capital allocation:
  - Cash/cash equivalents $2.55B at year‑end.
  - Operating cash flow $7.80B (down from $9.22B) on timing (F‑35 production/billing, receivables, 2021 inventory liquidation non‑repeat) and supplier accelerations ($1.5B outstanding at YE).
  - Free cash flow $6.13B; capex $1.67B (facilities, equipment, IT).
  - Dividends $3.0B ($11.40/share); share repurchases $7.9B (18.3M shares), including $4.0B ASR; remaining buyback authorization $10B.
  - New debt: $2.3B issued May 2022 (used to redeem 2023/2025 notes and part of 2026); $4.0B issued Oct 2022 (to fund ASR). Total debt (net) $15.5B; ample credit facility/commercial paper access.
- Contractual commitments and guarantees:
  - Total contractual cash obligations ~$96.5B; purchase obligations include ~$53.7B tied to U.S. Government contracts (termination for convenience framework applies).
  - Offset obligations ~$16.1B notional through 2044; potential penalties ~$1.8B; mix of cash and non‑cash fulfillment.
  - Standby letters of credit/surety bonds/guarantees outstanding ~$3.75B total.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Long‑term contract revenue recognition predominantly over time via percentage‑of‑completion cost‑to‑cost; variable consideration, contract modifications, and profit booking rate adjustments can materially affect period results.
  - CAS vs. FAS pension accounting; favorable FAS/CAS operating adjustment when CAS exceeds FAS service cost.
- Postretirement benefit plans:
  - Continued pension de‑risking via group annuity purchases; 2022 transfer of $4.3B obligations/assets generated $1.5B settlement charge; cumulative transfers since 2018 ~$15.9B.
  - Key assumptions: discount rate 5.25% (up from 2.875%), expected long‑term asset return 6.5%; 2022 asset return ~–18%. ERISA funded status ~82% (ARPA impact); no 2022/2021 cash contributions.
  - CAS pension cost recoveries $1.8B in 2022; prepayment credits ~$4.3B at YE.
- Environmental matters: Recorded liabilities $696M; probable recoveries from U.S. Government pricing $618M; long‑duration remediation with periodic reassessment; most costs allowable under FAR.
- Goodwill and intangibles: Goodwill $10.8B; annual impairment testing found no impairments; Sikorsky goodwill (approx. $2.7B) and trademark considered at higher risk if cash flows deteriorate; no COVID‑19 or inflation‑driven impairments anticipated.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: ITEM 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: We maintain active relationships with a broad and diverse group of U.S. and international financial institutions.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Item 7A—Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk, covering interest rate, foreign currency, and equity price risks, along with hedging, counterparty, and investment-related exposures.
- Credit access and counterparty management: Broad, diversified banking relationships; active monitoring of financial markets and counterparty exposure to ensure sufficient credit and mitigate single-counterparty risk.
- Interest rate risk: Exposure primarily from fixed-rate long-term debt and potential commercial paper. As of Dec 31, 2022, debt fair value $16.0B vs. $16.8B principal (excluding $1.3B discounts/issuance costs). A 10% rate change would not materially affect debt fair value.
- Foreign currency risk: Significant exposures to GBP, EUR, CAD, AUD, NOK, and PLN; use of forwards and options designated as cash flow hedges to manage forecasted FX transactions.
- Interest rate hedging: Use of swaps—fixed-to-variable (fair value hedges) and variable-to-fixed (cash flow hedges); may enter non-designated derivatives for economic hedges; no speculative trading.
- Derivative accounting and scale: Hedge effectiveness drives income statement vs. AOCI treatment; ineffectiveness recognized in earnings. Notional amounts at Dec 31—interest rate swaps $1.3B (2022) vs. $0.5B (2021) due to new Q4 debt; FX hedges $7.3B (2022) vs. $4.0B (2021) due to timing of foreign-denominated contract awards. Net derivative fair value not material. A 10% unfavorable FX move not material, with underlying exposures largely offsetting.
- Counterparty credit: Enter hedges only with acceptable-credit banks; diversified across many institutions; continuous monitoring; no trading/speculative derivatives.
- Deferred compensation trust: $1.6B at fair value (marketable equity and fixed-income) to fund non-qualified plans; related liabilities tied to company stock and market indices partially offset trust value changes; both recorded in “other unallocated, net” with immaterial 2022 impact.
- Equity price risk: Marketable securities of $24M; a 10% price decline would not be material. Non-marketable investments subject to broader market volatility affecting valuations, capital-raising prospects, and exit/liquidity outcomes (IPOs, mergers, private sales).

nodes.title: Revenue recognition based on the percentage of completion method
nodes.heading: Revenue recognition based on the percentage of completion method
nodes.start_phrase: Description of the MatterFor the year ended December 31, 2022 , the Corporation recorded net sales of $66.0 billion .
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines two critical audit matters for the year ended December 31, 2022. First, it explains that the corporation recognized most of its $66.0 billion in net sales from long-term contracts using the percentage-of-completion cost-to-cost method, which relies on estimate-at-completion analyses and significant management judgments about technical, schedule, and cost risks. These estimates affect profit booking rates and can materially impact results. The auditors evaluated internal controls over revenue recognition, tested management’s review processes and data integrity, compared estimated costs to historical results and contract terms, and performed sensitivity analyses on key assumptions. Second, it addresses the defined benefit pension plan obligation, noting a $28.7 billion obligation versus $23.2 billion in plan assets, resulting in a $5.5 billion net unfunded position. Measurement depends on actuarial valuations and key assumptions, particularly the discount rate, making the audit complex and requiring specialists.

nodes.title: Defined Benefit Pension Plan Obligation
nodes.heading: Defined Benefit Pension Plan Obligation
nodes.start_phrase: Description of the MatterAt December 31, 2022 , the Corporation’s aggregate obligation for its qualified defined benefit pension plans was $28.7 billion and exceeded the gross fair value of the related plan assets of $23.2 billion, resulting in a net unfunded qualified defined benefit pension obligation of $5.5 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Focus areas: Critical audit matters on revenue recognition for long-term contracts and measurement of defined benefit pension obligations, followed by audited consolidated financial statements (earnings, comprehensive income, balance sheet, cash flows, and equity) for 2020–2022.
- Revenue recognition (percentage-of-completion, cost-to-cost):
  - Majority of sales recognized over time using estimate-at-completion (EAC) analyses based on ratio of costs incurred to estimated total costs.
  - Profit booking rates adjust as technical, schedule, and cost risks are retired or increase; changes can materially impact results.
  - Audit addressed judgment and complexity by testing internal controls over EAC reviews, validating data completeness/accuracy, benchmarking labor/subcontract/material estimates to historicals and contracts, and performing sensitivity analyses on key assumptions.
- Defined benefit pension plan obligation:
  - At 12/31/2022, projected obligation $28.7b vs. plan assets $23.2b; net unfunded $5.5b. Plans are remeasured annually or upon certain events; discount rate is a key, judgmental actuarial assumption with significant impact.
  - Audit involved control testing over valuation, reviewing methods/assumptions and data, analyzing year-over-year changes (service cost, interest, payments, settlements, actuarial gains/losses, longevity, amendments), and using actuarial specialists to assess discount rate selection aligned to benefit cash flow maturities and testing participant data.
- Auditor: Ernst & Young LLP; auditor since 1994; Tysons, Virginia; report dated January 26, 2023.
- 2022 financial highlights:
  - Net sales: $66.0b (Products $55.5b; Services $10.5b); operating profit $8.35b; net earnings from continuing operations $5.73b; diluted EPS $21.66.
  - Other items: non-service FAS pension expense $(971)m; interest expense $(623)m; income tax expense $(948)m.
  - Other comprehensive income: $2.98b (driven largely by pension remeasurement and settlement effects); total comprehensive income $8.72b.
- Balance sheet at 12/31/2022:
  - Total assets $52.88b; key assets: cash $2.55b, receivables $2.51b, contract assets $12.32b, inventories $3.09b, PP&E net $7.98b, deferred taxes $3.74b.
  - Total liabilities $43.61b, including current liabilities $15.89b, long-term debt $15.43b (up vs. 2021), accrued pension liabilities $5.47b (down vs. 2021).
  - Stockholders’ equity $9.27b; accumulated other comprehensive loss $(8.02)b; decline in equity driven by share repurchases and dividends.
- Cash flows (2022):
  - Operating cash flow $7.80b; investing outflow $(1.79)b (capex $1.67b); financing outflow $(7.07)b driven by $7.90b in share repurchases and $3.02b dividends, partly offset by $6.21b net debt issuance; ending cash $2.55b.
- Equity movements (2020–2022):
  - Significant share repurchases in 2021–2022 and rising dividends ($11.40/share in 2022); OCI shifted to gains in 2021–2022 due to pension remeasurements; total equity decreased to $9.27b by year-end 2022.

nodes.title: Organization and Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.heading: Note 1 – Organization and Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.start_phrase: We are a global security and aerospace company principally engaged in the research, design, development, manufacture, integration and sustainment of advanced technology systems, products and services.
nodes.summary:
- Company overview: Lockheed Martin is a global security and aerospace company providing advanced technology systems and a wide range of services (management, engineering, technical, logistics, systems integration, cybersecurity) to U.S. and international customers, with the U.S. Government as the principal customer. Operations are organized into four segments: Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space.
- AWE program update: The UK Ministry of Defence renationalized the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) program on June 30, 2021; its operations were removed from Lockheed Martin’s results as of that date. AWE contributed $885 million of sales and $18 million of operating profit in 2021 (through June 30) and $1.4 billion of sales and $35 million of operating profit in 2020, all reported within the Space segment.
- Basis of presentation: Consolidated financial statements include controlled subsidiaries and variable interest entities where Lockheed Martin is the primary beneficiary; intercompany balances and transactions are eliminated. Certain assets and liabilities are classified as current based on the longer operating cycle of contracts/programs (affecting receivables, contract assets, inventories, contract liabilities), while other assets and liabilities use a one-year criterion.
- Use of estimates: Financial statements are prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP and require significant estimates, including for revenue and cost recognition; postretirement benefit plans; environmental liabilities and recoveries; impairment of goodwill, intangibles, investments, and other assets; income taxes and deferred taxes; fair value measurements; and contingencies. Actual results may differ materially from estimates.
- Revenue recognition: Most net sales arise from long-term contracts with the U.S. Government and international customers (including FMS). A contract is accounted for when mutual approval, identified rights and payment terms, commercial substance, and probable collectability exist; for certain international direct commercial sales requiring regulatory approvals, revenue is recognized when approvals are probable. Contract types include:
  - Fixed-price: Set pricing with profit/loss variability based on actual costs; may include performance-based incentives or penalties.
  - Cost-reimbursable: Reimbursement of allowable costs plus a fee (subject to funding ceilings), including cost-plus-award-fee (based on customer assessment of cost, quality, technical, schedule), cost-plus-incentive-fee (fee adjusted by formula relative to allowable costs), and cost-plus-fixed-fee.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition

- Basis of presentation: Consolidated subsidiaries and VIEs where LMT is primary beneficiary; intercompany eliminations; classification of certain current assets/liabilities based on contract operating cycle (often >1 year); all others based on one-year realization/settlement.
- Use of estimates: Significant judgments affect revenue/cost recognition, postretirement plans, environmental liabilities and recoveries, impairment of goodwill/intangibles/investments, income taxes and deferred taxes, fair value measurements, and contingencies.
- Revenue recognition:
  - Contract types: fixed-price (including incentives/penalties) and cost-reimbursable (cost-plus-award/incentive/fixed-fee).
  - Contract combination and identification of performance obligations; most contracts treated as a single performance obligation due to integration/complexity; some have multiple distinct obligations.
  - Transaction price includes variable consideration (awards/incentives/claims) measured at most likely amount, constrained to avoid significant reversals; options/modifications recognized when enforceable; most modifications treated as part of existing contracts.
  - Allocation to multiple performance obligations based on standalone selling price; for U.S. Government/FMS, FAR-based pricing typically equals standalone price; for non-U.S. Government, use expected cost plus margin or observable standalone sales when available.
  - Timing: Substantially all revenue recognized over time via percentage-of-completion cost-to-cost method due to continuous transfer of control (e.g., U.S. Government ownership/termination-for-convenience clauses or lack of alternative use plus right to payment). Point-in-time recognition used when control transfers at acceptance/delivery.
  - Backlog: $150.0 billion as of Dec 31, 2022; expected recognition of ~37% within 12 months, ~61% within 24 months, remainder thereafter; backlog may be adjusted for risk retirements without sales recognition.
  - Billing/payment terms: U.S. Government fixed-price typically PBPs or progress payments; cost-reimbursable billed monthly/semi-monthly for allowable costs plus fee; international direct commercial often advance and milestone payments.   - Estimation and profit effects: Ongoing reassessment of sales, costs, and variable consideration drives profit booking rates; recognize full reach-forward loss when estimated costs exceed transaction price. Favorable/unfavorable profit adjustments flow through current-period segment results.

Expense recognized net of estimated forfeitures over requisite service/vesting periods; adjust estimates each reporting date.
